title: Async Patterns, Web APIs & Live Coding

topics.title: Implement debounce and throttle. What's the difference?
topics.html:
// debounce — run once after the noise stops. Search input, autosave.
function debounce<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...a: A) => void, ms: number) {
  let t: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  const debounced = (...args: A) => {
    clearTimeout(t);
    t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(t);   // always offer cancel
  return debounced;
}

// throttle — run at most once per interval. Scroll, resize, mousemove.
function throttle<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...a: A) => void, ms: number) {
  let last = 0, timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined, lastArgs: A;
  return (...args: A) => {
    lastArgs = args;
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= ms) { last = now; fn(...args); }        // leading edge
    else if (!timer) {                                        // trailing edge
      timer = setTimeout(() => { last = Date.now(); timer = undefined; fn(...lastArgs); }, ms - (now - last));
    }
  };
}
  • Debounce waits for silence — the last call wins. Throttle guarantees a steady rate — the first call in each window wins.
  • In React, don't create them in the render body: they get recreated every render and the timer resets. Wrap in useMemo/useRef, or use a useDebouncedValue hook.
  • Always clean up on unmount, otherwise the callback fires against an unmounted component.
  • React alternative for input filtering: useDeferredValue — no timer, and it yields to urgent updates instead of guessing a delay.
// The React-idiomatic version
function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, ms = 300) {
  const [v, setV] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setTimeout(() => setV(value), ms);
    return () => clearTimeout(id);            // cleanup on every value change
  }, [value, ms]);
  return v;
}
💬 Say it like this

Debounce waits until the user stops. I use it for a search field so I do not send a request on every keystroke. Throttle sets a maximum frequency. I use it for scroll or resize so the handler runs at most once every hundred milliseconds. The detail people forget is cleanup: in React the timer must be cleared on unmount and on every change of the dependencies, otherwise you set state on a component that is already gone.

topics.title: Race conditions in data fetching — how do you cancel a request?
topics.html:
// The classic bug: fast type → two requests → the SLOW one resolves last and wins.
useEffect(() => {
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  fetch(`/api/search?q=${q}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
    .then(r => r.json())
    .then(setResults)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== "AbortError") setError(e); });
  return () => ctrl.abort();          // cleanup cancels the stale request
}, [q]);

// Timeout without a library
const withTimeout = (ms: number) => AbortSignal.timeout(ms);
await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.any([ctrl.signal, withTimeout(5000)]) });

// Ignore-flag variant when the API can't be aborted
useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  loadUser(id).then(u => { if (!ignore) setUser(u); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [id]);
  • Cancellation isn't only about network waste — it's about correctness. Without it, response order decides your state.
  • AbortError must be filtered out of error handling, or every cancelled request renders an error toast.
  • React Query does all of this for you: it passes a signal into the query function and keys the cache by query key, so stale responses can't overwrite fresh ones.
💬 Say it like this

The bug is that responses come back in a different order than the requests, so an old response overwrites a newer one. I fix it with AbortController: the cleanup of the effect cancels the previous request when the input changes. If the API cannot be cancelled, I use an ignore flag in the cleanup so the old result is dropped instead of going into state. In a real project React Query already does this for me.

Where else do stale updates bite you?
Any async work that touches state after an unmount or a param change: timers, subscriptions, animation callbacks, image decode. Same fix — the cleanup function owns the cancellation.

topics.title: Retry with exponential backoff, and limiting concurrency.
topics.html:
async function retry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, tries = 3, base = 300): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < tries; i++) {
    try { return await fn(); }
    catch (e) {
      if (i === tries - 1 || !isRetryable(e)) throw e;         // don't retry a 400
      const jitter = Math.random() * base;                      // avoid thundering herd
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, base * 2 ** i + jitter));
    }
  }
  throw new Error("unreachable");
}

// Run N promises at a time — uploading 200 files without killing the browser
async function pool<T, R>(items: T[], limit: number, fn: (t: T) => Promise<R>) {
  const results: R[] = [];
  const queue = [...items];
  const workers = Array.from({ length: limit }, async () => {
    while (queue.length) results.push(await fn(queue.shift()!));
  });
  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;
}
  • Only retry what is retryable: network errors, 429, 5xx. Retrying a 400 or a 401 just multiplies the failure.
  • Jitter matters — without it every client retries at the same millisecond and re-DDoSes the server it just recovered.
  • Mutations need idempotency (a request id) before you retry them, or you double-charge someone.
💬 Say it like this

I wait longer after every attempt and add a small random delay. I only retry errors that can succeed later — network errors, rate limits, server errors. A validation error will fail the same way forever. And I am careful with retrying mutations: if the endpoint is not idempotent, a retry can create a second order.

topics.title: Which browser APIs do you reach for instead of scroll handlers?
topics.html:
• IntersectionObserver — lazy loading, infinite scroll, "is this ad visible", scroll-spy. Runs off the main thread; no layout thrash.
  • ResizeObserver — element-level responsive behaviour without window resize listeners; the correct tool for container queries in JS.
  • MutationObserver — reacting to DOM changes you don't control (third-party widgets).
  • requestAnimationFrame — anything visual and per-frame. requestIdleCallback — non-urgent work like analytics flushes and prefetch.
  • Web Worker — genuinely heavy CPU work (parsing a large CSV, crypto, image processing) so the main thread keeps painting. Comlink makes the messaging bearable.
  • BroadcastChannel / storage event — sync state across tabs, e.g. logging out everywhere at once.
  • Page Visibility + navigator.sendBeacon — reliable analytics on unload.
const io = new IntersectionObserver(
  ([entry]) => { if (entry.isIntersecting) loadNextPage(); },
  { rootMargin: "200px" }        // start loading before it's actually visible
);
io.observe(sentinelRef.current!);
// React: create in useEffect, io.disconnect() in the cleanup
💬 Say it like this

My default is simple. If the question is "is this element visible", I use IntersectionObserver instead of a scroll listener — the browser does it more efficiently and I do not need to throttle anything. If the question is "did this element change size", I use ResizeObserver. And if something takes more than a few milliseconds of pure calculation, it goes into a web worker so the main thread can still react to the user.

topics.title: Small tasks that appear constantly.
topics.html:
// Deep clone — structuredClone handles Date, Map, Set, cycles. JSON.parse does not.
const copy = structuredClone(obj);        // no functions, no DOM nodes, no class identity

// Group an array
const byStatus = Object.groupBy(orders, o => o.status);      // modern
const byStatus2 = orders.reduce<Record<string, Order[]>>((acc, o) => {
  (acc[o.status] ??= []).push(o); return acc;
}, {});

// Flatten nested
const flat = arr.flat(Infinity);

// Unique by key
const uniq = [...new Map(items.map(i => [i.id, i])).values()];

// Safe get by path
const get = (o: any, p: string) => p.split(".").reduce((a, k) => a?.[k], o);

// Tiny event emitter — asked surprisingly often
class Emitter<E extends Record<string, unknown[]>> {
  private m = new Map<keyof E, Set<(...a: never[]) => void>>();
  on<K extends keyof E>(k: K, fn: (...a: E[K]) => void) {
    (this.m.get(k) ?? this.m.set(k, new Set()).get(k)!).add(fn as never);
    return () => this.off(k, fn);            // return the unsubscribe
  }
  off<K extends keyof E>(k: K, fn: (...a: E[K]) => void) { this.m.get(k)?.delete(fn as never); }
  emit<K extends keyof E>(k: K, ...a: E[K]) { this.m.get(k)?.forEach(f => (f as never as Function)(...a)); }
}
Interview habit: before you write a line, say the signature and one edge case out loud — "empty array, and I'll return the unsubscribe function". Interviewers score the approach more than the syntax.
💬 Say it like this

These are the small tasks that come up in almost every live coding round, so I try to know them without thinking.

The one worth mentioning out loud is deep clone: structuredClone handles dates, maps, sets and circular references, while the old JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) trick silently loses them.
